source.title: BehaveGPT: A Foundation Model for Large-scale User Behavior Modeling
source.authors: Jiahui Gong; Jingtao Ding; Fanjin Meng; Chen Yang; Hong Chen; Zuojian Wang; Haisheng Lu; Yong Li

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text and axes are garbled in the extraction, but the body text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Extends loss-scaling measurements to a user-behavior modeling domain rather than testing language models on text pretraining.
record.gate_note: The scaling section reports a fitted loss relationship, qualitative loss comparisons across data scales, and overfitting at larger model sizes. Other benchmark results and cited scaling-law findings are not rows because they do not measure scaling in this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains user-behavior transformers from scratch on Honor logs. It fits L(N,D) = C_N N^-α + C_D D^-β + L0 to its own runs, which bears on whether the power-law form holds outside text pretraining (V5). It does not study language-model text loss, extrapolation, fixed-compute allocation or shape.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely correct. The authors call the scaling study preliminary: loss improves with data and model size, and models trained from scratch overtake LLM-initialised ones as data grows. They also say limited data causes overfitting at larger sizes. They add that the data-to-model ratio (about 5) is far below that of LLMs, so behavior foundation models need less data. Note that their claim that α > β favours data scaling is stated without justification and is arguably inverted.
record.recipe_differences: Fits loss against model size and data size in user-behavior models, rather than measuring held-out language-model cross-entropy across parameters, tokens, and compute. The study does not test a fixed-compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Data size, model size, and whether the model uses pretrained language-model parameters or is trained from scratch; the text also reports overfitting when model size exceeds a threshold under limited data.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is described as preliminary. Numerical loss values are not stated in the prose, plotted scaling values are not recoverable from the garbled figure extraction, the overfitting threshold is unspecified, and uncertainty estimates are not reported. The paper does not state that the reported loss is held-out cross-entropy.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded downstream benchmark tables and DRO ablations because they do not measure scaling with model or data size. Excluded cited scaling-law results because they are not results of this study.

untested.parts: Only user-behavior next-event prediction on Honor data is tested. Image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning/transfer scaling are not tested. The scaling range is under two orders of magnitude in N.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation study. A data-to-model ratio is quoted but not tested as a power of compute.
No shape comparison at fixed N.
Downstream metrics are not related to scale or loss.

missing.what: The authors derive a data-to-model ratio of about 5 from Fig. 8(a) and compare it with Llama2 (70–100) and MiniCPM (about 192). They conclude the behavior domain needs far less data per parameter. This is a domain-dependence of the optimal split, relevant to V3 and V7, but it is not a tested compute-optimal frontier.
Fig. 7(a) loss values (axis about 2.7–3.3) for BehaveGPT-L/M/S, the no-DRO variant, GPT2 and Wukong-M across 50–600M records. These are unrecoverable from the extraction.

record.verdict_notes: The loss type is unspecified: the pretraining objective is DRO-weighted cross-entropy, and the text does not say whether the plotted loss is held-out. The text says 'fit the lossed' with curve_fit citing Hoffmann et al. No uncertainty is reported. V7 is removed from R1 and R4 because the study does not vary setup or fitting choices.

versions.untested_parts: The models are user-behavior models, not language models; the study does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss.
No small-run fit is evaluated as a prediction of the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study fits loss against model and data size, but does not compare parameter/token allocations at a fixed compute budget or test their growth with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Tests user-behavior data only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
It reports downstream task results, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
Reports one user-behavior-domain fit and overfitting with larger models under limited data. It does not systematically vary fitting choices or measure a fixed-compute optimal split.

rows.subject: BehaveGPT
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss as a function of model size N and data size D

conditions.value: six dataset sizes, from 1N to 10N; N denotes model size

rows.measure: Fitted loss relationship: L(N,D) = C_N N^(-α) + C_D D^(-β) + L0
rows.note: The authors say α is slightly larger than β and infer that data scaling should be emphasized slightly more than model scaling. The paper does not state that these losses are held-out cross-entropy.
rows.check: Drop V7: one fit in one domain varies no fitting choice. The range is narrow: three models (0.4M, 8M, 24M; about 1.8 orders of magnitude) and data from 1N to 10N. No goodness of fit is given. The authors' reading that α > β means data should be emphasised is the reverse of the usual reading of Eq. 5.

rows.subject: language-based model (the scaling figure labels GPT2)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained language-model initialization is discussed; exact setup for this comparison not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss as data size increases
rows.baseline: BehaveGPT loss; exact value not stated
rows.value: Lower loss than the behavior foundation model
rows.note: The prose describes the result for language-based models as a category and gives around 50M as an example; it does not identify a specific checkpoint in the prose.
rows.check: This compares a GPT-2-initialised model with BehaveGPT at about 50M records. It is a model-versus-model comparison, not a loss-versus-scale power law. The subject is the figure's 'GPT2' line, whose size is not stated.

rows.subject: BehaveGPT
rows.size_stated: not stated for the individual plotted model
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss as data size increases
rows.baseline: Language-based model loss; exact value not stated
rows.value: The behavior foundation model shows a sharper loss decline and ultimately outperforms the language-based model
rows.note: Qualitative result stated in the text; no exact loss values are provided.
rows.check: Qualitative only: the text says BehaveGPT loss falls more sharply with data, from 50M to 600M records. No numbers are given, and the power-law form is not assessed from this figure. The plotted sizes (L/M/S) are unreadable.

rows.subject: BehaveGPT
rows.size_stated: Model size surpassing a threshold; threshold not stated
rows.stage_stated: trained on the available behavior data
rows.operation_detail: Increase model size under limited data
rows.baseline: Performance before model size surpasses the unspecified threshold; exact value not stated
rows.value: The model begins to overfit the training set, reducing generalization ability and causing a sharp decline in performance
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative bend in performance but gives no threshold or numerical measurements.
rows.check: Should link to V5, not V7. Under fixed limited data, performance declines sharply beyond an unstated model size, which the monotonic Eq. 5 form cannot represent. This is a data-bottleneck regime. The measure is 'generalization performance' with no number or threshold, from Fig. 7(b).

relationships.condition: BehaveGPT trained from scratch on Honor user-behavior logs, 0.4M–24M params, data 1N–10N
relationships.reason: A Chinchilla-form additive power law is fitted with α=0.51, β=0.23 (R1), and loss falls with data up to 600M records (R3). The range is narrow and no fit quality is reported.
relationships.display_finding: An additive Chinchilla-form fit yielded α=0.51 and β=0.23, while loss decreased with data through 600M records, without reported fit quality.

relationships.condition: Model sizes above an unstated threshold with limited Honor data
relationships.reason: The authors report overfitting and a sharp performance decline as model size grows under fixed data (R4). This departs from a monotonic power law in N. The report is qualitative.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing model size beyond a threshold caused overfitting and a sharp performance decline under fixed data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: BehaveGPT trained on Honor user-behavior data
reader_labels.reason: The study fits loss against both model and data size and reports fitted exponents for this domain (R1); it also reports loss improving with increased data and a comparison changing with data scale (R2–R3). This supports only the tested user-behavior setting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: BehaveGPT at model sizes beyond an unspecified threshold under limited data
reader_labels.reason: The authors report overfitting and a sharp decline in generalization performance as model size exceeds a threshold (R4); a single power-law account therefore needs qualification in this setting.
